newsitem.title: USA: Clinton offers cooperation, faces tough fights.
newsitem.headline: Clinton offers cooperation, faces tough fights.

text.p: Although President Bill Clinton began his second term offering to end political bickering with Republicans -- and having them accept it -- tough, bruising battles clearly lie ahead.

Calling for a truce in the war zone mentality that has besieged much of Washington during the past two years of Republican control of Congress, Clinton spoke of cooperation in his second inaugural address.

Citing the decision of voters to put a Democrat in the White House and Republicans in charge of Congress, Clinton said, "Surely they did not do this to advance the politics of petty bickering and extreme partisanship."
"No, they call on us instead to be repairers of the breach and to move on with America's mission," he said.
Although Republicans quickly agreed with Clinton's message of cooperation, they still have problems with his mission.
Trying to avoid criticism that he was embracing symbolism but not offering substance, Clinton caught many by surprise by taking the lead in dealing with cutting the budget deficit.
He proposed $138 billion in Medicare savings over six years -- tackling a politically dangerous issue Republicans had accused him of avoiding.
"I want to meet them halfway on this and on many other issues, and I hope they will meet me halfway," said Clinton, who initially generated positive reaction from Republicans.
By week's end, however, Republicans were saying Clinton still has miles to go before he meets them halfway.

California Republican Representative Bill Thomas, chairman of the House Ways and Means subcommittee that oversees Medicare, called some aspects of the president's plan little more than a "gimmick" that fell far short of true reform of the system.
The opening salvo in the budget debate shows that a wide rift remains in the battle over control of the purse strings and programmes of the federal government.

Clinton will outline his agenda during a Feb. 4 State of the Union address to a joint session of Congress and then detail how he would carry it out when he submits his budget plan for the next fiscal year on Feb. 6.

Clinton encountered swift Senate confirmation of Madeleine Albright as the first woman to serve as secretary of state and William Cohen, a former Republican senator from Maine, as secretary of defence.
Clear sailing does not lie ahead, however, for Anthony Lake, the White House national security adviser who was Clinton's choice to head the Central Intelligence Agency.
Some critics blame him for the administration's failure to notify Congress that it was secretly allowing Iran to break an arms embargo and supply weapons to Bosnian Moslems.
Clinton confidants say he intends to be an activist president as he crafts policies and positions that someday will be used by historians to assess his record.
"He doesn't want to be remembered just for stopping the Republicans," said one adviser, refering to past battles that ended in stalemate or veto -- and twice shut the federal government.
"He really believes he can work with the Republicans, especially now that their attitudes have changed," the administration official said.

White House officials say they expect the ethical problems that have hounded House Speaker Newt Gingrich -- along with his low standing in most opinion polls -- will give the Senate Gingrich was not expected to loom over the political stage and dominate the agenda the way he has in the past.
One official said Senate Republican leader Trent Lott, although a staunch conservative, "is someone we can work with ... (it) shouldn't be impossible to find a compromise."
Another administration official noted that the first year of a president's second term offers "a real opportunity" for accomplishment because political pressures are not as intense.
"We're in a legacy mode," the official said, referring to the fact that Clinton can accomplish nothing without Republican support.
